Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

My thought on the role of growth in solving fiscal problems:

1. I'm in favor of dynamic scoring for both tax & spending plans--you should take into account the best estimate of impact on budget.

2. Dynamic scoring needs to be done by CBO/JCT, they're generally unbiased and reasonably efficient. As a result they often disappoint advocates.

3. Ideally CBO would also display other information than just growth, the sole goal of every policy is not necessarily growth, it might also be about providing health insurance or increasing national security.

4. Dynamic scoring will usually be small relative to the first order effects of policies on spending and taxes.

5. I wouldn't overthink the second-order political incentives and impacts, if you have good information you'll generally (but not always) have better policy.

Economic worries typically dominate midterm elections, and 2026 is no different. The affordability question, which directly ties to the economy and direction of the country, appears to be the core issue driving voter sentiment.

What is notable this year is how 4 foreign policy issues have affected those economic issues. CFR experts break down how the Iran war, U.S. trade policy, AI, and immigration could be shaping voters’ perceptions of the economy and the United States’ role in the world.

Among voters, there is a “lack of enthusiasm about continuing involvement in Middle East wars,” said CFR expert Elliott Abrams. They sense that foreign wars divert resources from domestic needs and, more importantly, have started to feel a “direct and immediate” economic effect, Abrams added.

A CFR poll authored by CFR's Allison Smith found that Americans understood tariffs to raise prices of not only goods but also services. Smith said that this could have an effect on voter sentiment. “Consumers are definitely making the connection between tariffs and the higher prices that they’re paying,” she said.

CFR expert Pierre Yared pointed to the COVID-19 pandemic and the U.S. housing shortage as true drivers of the affordability crisis. “Voters’ concerns come from the sticker shock from the cumulative inflation they experienced after the pandemic, which is still around since the price level has not come back down,” Yared said.

Immigration and immigration policy remain important issues in the 2026 midterms. “I don’t think that American voters were prepared for what the Trump administration has delivered, and I think that’s what you’re seeing in the polls now,” Edward Alden, a CFR senior fellow specializing in immigration policy, said. American voters want a sense that the U.S. government is maintaining control over immigration, he added.

Voter mood around AI heading into the midterms is “more anxious than enthusiastic,” CFR technology and national security expert Jessica Brandt said. The adoption of AI tools has increased the share of Americans who fear that the technology could cause their jobs to become obsolete, and public polling indicates that voters are connecting data center buildouts nationwide to rising electricity bills.

I'm now building an "improvements" feature into all of my personal vibecoded applications: a freeform text input that's hooked up to an agent that yolo implements whatever is submitted.

It's an interesting experience -- the activation energy barrier to sanding any rough edge or implementing any new feature becomes extremely low. Someone else who uses one of the applications I created has already implemented 150 improvements over the course of a few days. This pattern feels like a new kind of tool -- liquid software? -- and every application that doesn't have this feature now has a slightly rigid and anachronistic flavor. Why can't I just tell it how I want it to be different?

Now, it's not obvious to me how this pattern can or should scale. Does it become unmaintainable after a while? (Maybe model intelligence improvement outstrips my feature appetite such that it's fine?) How does collaborative software work in this model? Can software designed this way be secure and reliable?

Whatever the larger questions about broader deployment, it definitely works great in a personal context. It reminds me a little of the visions of Lisp/Lisp machines, Smalltalk, and HyperCard -- systems that the user can take control of and modify. Those visions never quite worked, though: the vast majority of software today is not end-user modifiable in any useful way. So, while this "liquid" affordance is a very small touch, the way it changes one's relation to the software feels a bit transgressive and empowering in a Lickliderian and Engelbartian way.

How many people struggle with mental health issues?

Could this become a new recurring revenue engine?

What is Blaze?

Blaze is E2E's new pay-per-token AI inference platform, built on NVIDIA DSX OS.

It offers:
• A single OpenAI-compatible API to access models including NVIDIA Nemotron, Sarvam, DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM and Gemma.
• Inference infrastructure for coding agents, document AI, OCR, image and video generation.
• NVIDIA CUDA kernels and Dynamo-based serving.
• An India-hosted AI infrastructure option for enterprises requiring data residency.
In simple terms, developers can access multiple AI models through one platform without building and managing their own GPU infrastructure.

WHY IS THIS STRATEGICALLY IMPORTANT?
There are three layers to E2E's opportunity:
GPU infrastructure.

GPU hosting and managed computing.

AI inference and production deployment.

The third layer could be particularly interesting because it creates an opportunity to monetise GPU capacity repeatedly through customer consumption.

Higher GPU utilisation → More tokens processed → Potentially higher recurring revenue.

THE INFRASTRUCTURE BEHIND THIS

E2E has highlighted approximately 14.6 MW of AI factory capacity.

Its infrastructure includes:
• A 1,024-GPU NVIDIA Blackwell cluster, live since May 2026.
• An additional 5.4 MW of Blackwell capacity, including HGX B300 systems and other Blackwell GPUs.

The company also offers TIR alongside Blaze.

Blaze: API-based, token-efficient AI inference.

TIR: Self-hosted inference, model pre-training and post-training on managed GPU clusters.

This allows E2E to address both developers looking for simple API access and enterprises wanting greater control over their AI infrastructure.|

Rising inference demand: AI agents and enterprise applications moving into production could increase recurring token consumption.

Higher GPU utilisation: Monetising installed Blackwell capacity could improve infrastructure productivity.

Sovereign AI demand: Banks, healthcare providers, enterprises and public-sector organisations may prefer India-hosted AI infrastructure with greater data control.

The announcement is strategically important, but actual commercial traction will determine its financial impact.

Watch:
• Paying inference customers.
• Tokens processed and revenue per token.
• GPU utilisation.
• Revenue contribution from Blaze and TIR.
• Gross margins and cash generation.
• Capital expenditure required for additional capacity.

E2E Networks is attempting to move higher up the AI value chain.

Instead of merely renting out expensive GPUs, it wants to monetise the entire AI computing cycle — from model training to inference and production deployment.

If Blaze gains customer traction, it could create a recurring, consumption-led revenue stream and improve returns from the company's substantial GPU investments.

The biggest question is no longer just how many GPUs E2E owns. It is how productively those GPUs can be monetised.

As an AI/ML Engineer, you must build these projects.

1.) Custom Triton Kernel
Build:  A fused RMSNorm or RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) kernel in Triton, benchmarked against native PyTorch.

Why: Python overhead and memory reads kill inference. You cannot optimize what you treat as a black box.

2.) Synthetic Data Curation Engine
Build:  A pipeline using a frontier model to generate 50k complex logic traces, filtered by a deterministic verifier for training.

Why:  The internet is out of human text. High-quality, verifiable synthetic data is the ultimate training moat.

3.) MinHash Deduplication Pipeline
Build:  A scalable script that scans terabytes of pre-training data and removes near-duplicates using MinHash and LSH.

Why:  Training on duplicates causes memorization, destroys model generalization and wastes compute.

4.) QLoRA + TIES Model Merger
Build:  Fine-tune a 70B model in 4-bit on a single 24GB GPU, then merge it with the base model using TIES to resolve gradient conflicts.

Why:  Full fine-tuning is dead for 99% of teams. PEFT and merging are how you adapt frontier intelligence cheaply.

5.) KTO Alignment Flywheel
Build:  Align an SFT model using Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO) on binary "good/bad" signals without needing paired preference data.

Why:  SFT teaches what to say. Alignment teaches how to behave, and KTO slashes human annotation costs.

6.) FSDP Multi-GPU Training Harness
Build:  A custom training loop sharding a 7B model across 4 GPUs using Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) and gradient checkpointing.

Why:  Single-GPU training is for tutorials. Production research requires sharding weights without bottlenecking the interconnect.

7.) Sparse MoE Routing Layer
Build:  A Mixture of Experts router from scratch with a load-balancing auxiliary loss to prevent expert collapse.

Why:  Sparse MoE is the architecture behind the smartest models. Naive routing destroys their latency advantage.

8.) Vision-Language Projection Head
Build:  A lightweight MLP mapping SigLIP vision embeddings into an LLM's text embedding space for custom visual reasoning.

Why:  Text is only half the internet. Fusing modalities natively is mandatory for 2026 applications.

9.) Automated Red-Team Fuzzer
Build:  An adversarial agent using tree-of-thought prompting to systematically find jailbreaks and edge cases in your safety classifier.

Why: Static benchmarks are easily gamed. You must build harnesses that continuously attack your own models.

10.) AWQ Quantization & Perplexity Tracker
Build:  Calibrate a model to 4-bit AWQ, measure the exact perplexity degradation, and benchmark latency gains in vLLM.

Why:  Quantization is the only way to fit frontier models on edge GPUs and protect cloud margins.

11.) W&B Automated Hyperparameter Sweep
Build:  A Ray cluster integrated with Weights & Biases that automatically searches learning rates and weight decays based on validation loss.

Why:  Manual tuning is guessing. Automated sweeps find the mathematical optimum for your specific data mix.

12.) Semantic Complexity Router
Build:  An inference gateway that analyzes prompt entropy to route simple queries to a local 8B and complex reasoning to a 70B API.

Why:  Unit economics decide if your AI product survives. Routing protects your margins.

13.) Custom Autograd Activation Function
Build:  A novel non-linear activation function with a manually written forward and backward pass in C++/CUDA.

Why:  You cannot debug a collapsing loss curve if you rely entirely on PyTorch's `autograd` black box.

14.) Speculative Decoding Pipeline
Build:  A serving setup where a local 2B draft model proposes tokens for a 70B target model to verify in a single forward pass.

Why:  2x decode speed at zero quality loss is the closest thing to a free lunch in inference.

15.) Arxiv Reproduction & HuggingFace Release
Build:  Reproduce a brand-new paper in <500 lines of PyTorch, publish the weights, the training logs and a teardown of the results.

Why:  Top AI labs hire ML Engineers based on their public repos and training methodologies not their degrees.

Taiwanese parents who moved to Arizona with TSMC are worried that American education is not challenging enough. One mother associated with the chipmaker had moved there because she wanted an easier academic environment for her son.

As writer Dan Wang (@danwwang) reported in the New York Times this month, the company's engineers have found that their kids consider American classes far less challenging than those in Taiwan, and that math and science classes are a breeze. This is causing consternation among these parents.

Wang Yi-ping was an award-winning teacher in Tainan, in southern Taiwan, and her husband is a manager at TSMC's Arizona plant. When the transfer was first mentioned, she would have nothing to do with it. Her oldest son convinced her to change her mind.

He went to one of the most competitive public schools in the south, where before dawn every morning chartered buses arrived carrying the best students from Tainan and the nearby city of Kaohsiung. "If you aren't willing to put in extra for scores, you're weeded out," she told Global Views magazine.

Before his ninth-grade national exam, she dropped him off at cram school. She had barely gotten home when the teaching assistant called. Her son had said he was going out to the convenience store and never came back. The school called at least three times to ask why he wasn't in class. He had stayed home.

He went abroad for a year as an exchange student, to Wisconsin, and when he came back, he said to her, "Mom, I found out studying is just one of the important things." In Phoenix, his grades rose, and now he asks her to pick him up late after class so that he can stay behind and ask his teachers questions.

Taiwan's results on international tests show the benefit and the cost of such an education. In the most recent big international math test, 44% of Taiwan's eighth graders reached the highest proficiency level, compared with 8% of Americans. But 61% of the Taiwanese students surveyed said that they did not like studying math, compared with 51% of American students.

Taiwan gets some of the highest math scores in the world by putting all its children into the same race, competing for the same test scores. Among the other TSMC parents in Phoenix, there is fear that their children will fall behind in that race. Wang Yi-ping moved her son to get him out of that race, because, in Taiwan's system, if a child is not right for that race then he does not have an alternative track. this is part of neuralink's voice trial, re: whether a brain implant can turn attempted speech into a synthesized voice. 30 versions of this app were tested in 3 days

after integrating bloom with iphone calling, bci-generated speech is now injected directly into call's microphone giving the person on the other end clear audio. this is essentially a hackathon translating thought to speech

lots of respect from the team to kenneth and family on opening up their home, giving feedback, and allowing everyday folks like us to be able to learn what's possible at the frontier. we hope to cover more stories like this on @MTSlive

WHOEVER LEAKED THIS JEV BRAIN SCAN DESERVES THE BCI CHAIR

I thought a brain scan was one grayscale picture, two findings, and a bill from your HMO.

Apparently not.

This scan's setup is much more interesting:

→ ANATOMY splits the volume across 6 regions (frontal 12.3, parietal 12.0, temporal 14.6, occipital 9.9, cerebellum 7.2, brainstem 4.5 percent), no averaging across the whole brain
→ PATHWAYS tracks 5 named signal routes (corticospinal 95, arcuate 86, uncinate 75, fornix 67, cingulum 63 percent), each pathway logged separately, no "overall connectivity" lie
→ EEG BANDS resolves delta 1.2 Hz, theta 4.8, alpha 10.0, beta 18.3, gamma 34.4 continuously, no manual channel re-reference
→ NEUROTRANSMITTERS tracks dopamine 58, serotonin 67, norepinephrine 56, acetylcholine 62, GABA 51 in parallel, no snapshot bias
→ PROCESSING UNITS surfaces live load per cognitive module (visual 97, auditory 65, motor 67, executive 96, default mode 63 percent), flags 6 modules drifting past the baseline this scan

so you get:

Regions resolved. Pathways tracked. Bands continuous. Modules loaded.

the interesting part isn't a higher-res scan.
it's giving every signal a layer the atlas can anchor against the next session.

Instead of a radiologist reading one picture and writing "within normal limits", you load 86.5B neurons at 4.2ms processing, resolve 5 EEG bands live, and read neurotransmitter levels across 5 systems in the same scan.

Resolve the region. Track the pathway. Load the module.
